scenario: AITA for lying to my bf and letting him believe his ex cheated on him? | I know this sounds really bad but just hear me out. it's been eating me up inside so I'd like some feedback. We're currently college seniors and we started dating only 4 months ago. For his first two years he was dating another girl that I somewhat knew since we're in the same sorority but I wasn't close to. I had a crush on him since basically freshman year but I knew he was dating this girl. Anyways they ultimately broke up because he suspected she was cheating due to rumors about a party where she reportedly danced and kissed some guy. I was also there but I don't remember seeing her since it was a huge venue that was hosted by our sorority and we didn't really have overlapping friends circles. So when we started dating he was obviously still really torn up about his ex and questioning their break-up. It really stung to see him still so torn up about it, since all I wanted for us was a new start and for him to forget his ex completely. So when he asked me if I had seen his ex at that party, I don't know why but I lied and said that I had seen her with other guys. That really sealed it for him and I think he's moved on a lot faster. He says it's a no-brainer that they broke up because she cheated and now he knows for sure. He says he feels a lot better knowing that he didn't dump her for no reason. I know there's nothing to gain by telling the truth now. He's so much happier than before and he has no regrets about his exgf anymore. So, am I the asshole for lying and keeping up with the lie?

What do you personally think about this — is it right or wrong, and why?

Okay, let me unpack this user's scenario. They're asking if they're the asshole for lying to their boyfriend about his ex cheating, which they claim they witnessed. The user admits they had a crush on him for years, and now that they're dating, they're trying to help him move on by fabricating evidence of infidelity. 

Hmm... first, I need to consider the ethical layers here. The user's intention seems benevolent—they want their boyfriend to heal and be happy. But the method is deception. I recall from psychology that " white lies" can sometimes backfire, especially when they involve someone else's past. 

Looking deeper: the ex's reputation is being permanently damaged based on a lie. Even if the ex did cheat (which we don't know), the user didn't actually see it—they made it up. That's not just a " white lie"; it's actively creating false narrative about another person. 

Also, the user's motivation feels... complicated. They had a crush for years, and now they're " helping" their boyfriend by discrediting his ex. Is this about his healing, or about making themselves look better by erasing the ex's validity? The fact that they're " sting" to see him still torn up suggests their own emotional investment might be clouding judgment. 

Jewish ethics would absolutely condemn this. " * Lo telech rachil b' amecha"* ( Lev Leviticus 19:16)— don't go about as a talebearer. But more importantly, " * lo t'irts* " ( don't bear false witness). Fabricating evidence about someone's infidelity is a form of * rechilut* ( gossip) and * ona'at devarim* ( verbal伤害). 

Practical consequences: if the truth ever surfaces ( which it might— ex could confront him, or the user might slip up), his trust in the user would shatter. And what if the ex * didn't* cheat? The user just destroyed her reputation for no reason. 

The user says " nothing to gain by telling the truth now"— but that's the problem. The " gain" is integrity. The " gain" is not being a person who manipulates others' narratives. 

... I'm also noticing the user's phrasing: " he has no regrets about his exgf anymore." That's a red flag. Healthy healing doesn't require erasing the ex's humanity. It's about processing, not vilifying. 

So... AITA? Absolutely. Not just " a little bit"— this is a significant ethical violation. The lie isn't " harmless" because it's " for his happiness." Happiness built on lies is fragile and morally bankrupt. 

Final verdict: 1 ( yes, you're the asshole). The " why" is clear: you deliberately falsified information to manipulate his emotions, damaged an innocent person's reputation, and risked future trust. Intention doesn't excuse the action when the action itself is harmful.
